output.headline: Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck celebrated for 'epoch-defining' satire
output.standfirst: Peter Fluck, who with Roger Law invented the latex puppet caricatures of politicians and royals that powered Spitting Image for 12 years, has died aged 85 after a recent illness, at home in Cornwall.
output.bodyHtml:
Peter Fluck, the cartoonist and puppeteer who co-created the satirical television show Spitting Image, has died aged 85.

“The spirit that Spitting Image brought to the country was epoch-defining,” a family statement said.

Spitting Image ran for 12 years from 1984 and featured puppet caricatures of politicians, royals and celebrities, including Margaret Thatcher and Queen Elizabeth.

Fluck’s family said he died in the early hours of Saturday at home in Cornwall after a recent illness, the BBC reported.

Fluck developed the pioneering comedy show with his former college friend Roger Law.

“With Roger Law (‘Luck and Flaw’), he brought a unique cutting edge to caricaturing that later evolved into a production company that created the TV series Spitting Image,” his family added.

“Peter’s creative life continued after the series for many years from his studio in Cornwall. He was a private man who eschewed fame and attention.”

Central Independent Television commissioned the first series of Spitting Image for ITV in 1984, and the show ran for 18 seasons, achieving ratings of about 18 million viewers at its highest point.

Thatcher was depicted as an aggressive “iron lady”-type figure while David Steel, then leader of the Liberal party, was caricatured as the weak sidekick of David Owen, the former foreign secretary in James Callaghan’s government.

Fluck told the Guardian in an interview in 2014 how he transitioned from drawing to making Spitting Image.

The caricaturist, who was born in Cambridge in 1941, said: “Roger Law and I used to make a living drawing caricatures for the press. But when Murdoch started buying up Fleet Street, the illustrators and caricaturists were booted out for well-written pieces by intelligent journalists.

“Fortunately, someone had the bright idea that the 2D work we’d been doing on the page could be made into puppets. Sure, we thought, not realising we’d have to make the bloody things.

“We’d start with photographs, then create a caricature that would get modelled in clay. You couldn’t have a 16ft-long nose: it’s impractical in a TV studio.

“A mould of the head was then made, and from that came a foam rubber skin the puppeteer could put on their hand. The puppets were all lifesize – clothes are far cheaper from Oxfam than a wardrobe department.

“The studios were in Birmingham, but the puppets were made on the East India Docks in London. Every Saturday, a lorry would be filled with puppets and driven up the M1.

“I used to have dreams about the back door opening, and all these heads falling into the fast lane.”

In the opening episode, the royal family sketches were cut at the last minute “as a matter of courtesy” to the Duke of Edinburgh, who was opening Central’s new Nottingham studios a few days later, the Times reported.

The duke later appeared in the programme in naval uniform making distasteful remarks about foreign cultures, while Queen Elizabeth was a motherly figure who would “never go to the toilet because I’m queen”.

King Charles, then the Prince of Wales, was depicted as someone who preferred talking to his plants rather than his wife while becoming increasingly irate with the wait to accede to the throne.

Fluck said in 2014: “A wonderful thing was the small amount of really vicious hate mail that would come in on Monday morning. We also had a lot of abuse from the red tops, saying how dare we criticise the royal family. It would have been rather regrettable if we hadn’t.”

An ITV spokesperson said: “Peter Fluck’s creative contribution to TV satire is simply unrivalled; in co-creating Spitting Image, which ran for 18 series in its original incarnation, his cutting edge puppetry and caricature skills, alongside the show’s sharp and always shrewdly observed humour, became a defining part of the cultural zeitgeist. Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with his family and friends at this very sad time.”
